messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Layla, at seventy-seven, carried a stillness that seemed out of place in the cheerful, cluttered homes where she tutored children in mathematics. The trauma was from a lifetime ago, another country, but its architecture remained, structuring her days. It happened during the war, on an afternoon that had felt deceptively ordinary. She had been in a small bakery, the air thick with the scent of cardamom, when the world outside the shop window dissolved into a cascade of white light and roaring sound. The building across the street collapsed into a cloud of dust and debris, the shockwave shattering the bakery’s windows and throwing her to the floor amidst the broken glass and scattered pastries. She remembers the screaming, the sudden darkness as the dust blotted out the sun, and a profound, animal terror that she was about to be buried alive.

In the years since resettling in America, that moment has never truly ended. She describes how something as simple as a car backfiring or a dropped crate at the grocery store can instantly bring back the full memory, not as a recollection, but as a lived reality. When this happens, she feels the same raw terror she felt on the bakery floor, a certainty that her life is ending. It is not like watching a film of the past; she feels the grit of dust in her mouth and the paralyzing fear that the ceiling is about to give way. This is why she has come to believe, with unshakeable conviction, that she is a weak person. The strength and resilience she once prided herself on feel like a memory of someone else. Now, she is certain that if she allows herself to truly think about the event, to let the memories in voluntarily, she will not be able to handle it. She imagines a complete shattering, a loss of self from which she would never return.

This core belief that she is too fragile to cope governs her every move. At the homes of her students, she will politely but firmly insist on being seated in the chair closest to the front door, ensuring her path to an exit is always clear. Her students’ parents see it as a quirk of an elderly woman, but for Layla, it is a non-negotiable condition for her safety. She has also systematically purged her life of potential reminders. She never watches the news or reads the paper, and if a film on television so much as hints at conflict or disaster, she immediately turns it off. This avoidance extends to her inner world; she spends hours dwelling on how she used to be before the event, looking at old photographs of a vibrant, smiling woman she no longer recognizes as herself. This rumination on a lost past is her safest way of touching her own history without getting too close to the part that burned it all down.

The conviction that her memories are unmanageable has, paradoxically, given them more power. Because she regards any flicker of the trauma as a sign of imminent collapse, the memories themselves arrive steeped in a secondary layer of terror. The thought “I can’t handle this” is the usher that announces their arrival, and this anticipatory dread makes the reliving experience feel even more vivid and threatening, confirming her belief that the memory itself is dangerous. The strategies she uses to protect herself also conspire against her. By refusing to watch news of current events or read about similar tragedies, she prevents herself from ever contextualizing her experience. As a result, when a sudden noise triggers a flashback, it comes without warning, a raw sensory fragment untethered to any narrative. The memory crashes into her consciousness with the full force of the original event precisely because she has worked so hard to keep the door to that part of her mind sealed.

This cycle of avoidance and intrusion has become the central proof of her own perceived weakness. Each time she has to reposition a chair to be near a door, she feels a hot flush of shame, a confirmation that she is no longer a capable person. Each evening she spends avoiding television and instead dwelling on the past reinforces the chasm between who she was and the frightened woman she has become. Her strategies are no longer just about safety; they are a constant, running commentary on her own inadequacy. This has left her with a pervasive feeling of being dead inside, a profound emotional numbness that blankets everything. It is this feeling, more than the fear, that finally brought her to therapy. The thick pane of glass between herself and the world has become unbearable. She is terrified of revisiting the memory, but the thought of living out the rest of her years as a ghost in her own life has become, at last, even more frightening.
